title: Special Issue: Why America Needs a Third Founding
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/jay-tolson
text:
As regular readers of this periodical know, the Institute for Advanced Studies in Culture at the University of Virginia is both the home and publisher of The Hedgehog Review. As a happy consequence, each of our issues during our twenty-seven years of publication reflects the Institute’s guiding concern with cultural change in the modern world. By that widely used word culture, we specifically mean the sphere of human society concerned with meanings, values, beliefs, and customs, as all are formulated, reflected, modified, and contested in realms ranging from popular culture, the arts, and the media to organized religion, education, law, science and technology, and the institutions and practices of commerce.

Add to those, of course, the most troubled precinct of contemporary American life—the political sphere.

It is no overstatement to say that the forces undercutting the institutions of republican government and the norms and ideals of liberal democracy are in alarming ascendancy in the United States. Some even say they have prevailed—that we the people have failed to uphold the commission implied by Benjamin Franklin when asked what form of government the Constitutional Convention had created: “A republic, if you can keep it.” How well are we keeping it when so many US citizens seem indifferent, if not resigned, to the shameless efforts of a few to dismantle the mechanisms of democracy for personal power or financial gain, or to realize political advantage by stoking the fires of division?

Yet while individual politicians and political parties have contributed directly, and sometimes decisively, to the current crisis of democratic governance, it is the firm conviction and intellectual consensus of the Institute that the deeper problem is cultural—and that the foundations of our political system in our political culture have been eroding for decades. That decline has been a topic of concern for the Institute ever since its founding in 1995, becoming even more urgent during the past ten years. That sense of urgency led the Institute’s founder and executive director, James Davison Hunter, following up on the argument of his 2024 book, Democracy and Solidarity: On the Cultural Roots of America’s Political Crisis, to launch an initiative, involving the diverse intellectual talents of the Institute’s community of scholars, to consider why our political culture no longer seems to provide citizens with a shared and binding sense of those norms that are essential to keeping a republic.

Dubbing it the Third Founding, Hunter envisioned the initiative to be both a focus of scholarly investigation and a plan of action for networked civic engagement aimed at reconsidering and adapting for our own time the principles, ideals, norms, and often tacit beliefs undergirding our liberal democratic republic. This call for renewed engagement with America’s unwritten constitution (the prerequisite to the written Constitution) is intended to respond to the challenges, inconsistencies, and contradictions of our political order in ways just as radical as did the First Founding (the Revolution of 1776 and the ratification of the Constitution in 1788) by transforming royal British Colonial subjects into citizens of a democratic and independent nation; and as did the Second Founding (coming after the Civil War, with a commitment to fulfilling the selectively denied egalitarian promise of the First Founding) by launching more than a century of bipartisan efforts to extend true equality—not only before the law but also with respect to opportunity—to all American citizens.

Today, the promises of the American creed are being seen, from different partisan, class, ethnic, or regional perspectives, as unfulfilled, broken, hollow, or even meaningless. Americans, more diverse than ever, are quarreling over the meanings and interpretations of what were once our most cherished ideals and institutions, including liberty, equality, citizenship, federalism, democracy, free speech, the rule of law, and even the nation itself.

Making matters worse, the civil-society institutions long recognized for their indispensable role in upholding and inculcating democratic ideals and practices, as well as the norms of a shared civic life—including churches and universities, business corporations and trade unions, the press, and the many professions—are now either politicized or diminished, abandoned or neglected, and, as a result, often viewed with skepticism or suspicion. That distrust extends to even the broadest and deepest sources of authority, religion and science, whose respective truth claims are not only misstated by their proponents but pitted against each other in simplistic misconceptions of what each magisterium is capable (or incapable) of asserting. The result is an impoverishment of public morality and public reason, as well as the debasement of the principle of secularity as the guarantor of freedom of belief.

In the meanwhile, popular culture either degrades or further divides the public, while the newest digital technologies threaten to replace human agency with all-knowing AI. And as the income gap widens, the prospect of a new Gilded Age class of the ultra-wealthy poses direct threats to democratic governance while shortsighted and often badly governed business corporations dedicated to shareholder value alone ignore their founding public purpose and even the well-being of their own organizations. With such an ethical hollowing out of our institutions, is it any wonder that so many are now asking if democracy’s center can hold?

The urgency of this broad cultural collapse—marked by what Hunter describes as the triumph of nihilism—gave rise not just to this special issue of The Hedgehog Review, whose essays address many of the issues named above, but also to the Third Founding initiative itself. The inaugural declaration of this initiative appears at the outset of the thematic section.

Beyond cultural critique, the Third Founding is an invitation to leaders and participants in our diverse civil society to join in a shared effort to renew America’s political culture, an effort distinctive in six ways:

First: Committed to nonpartisanship, the Third Founding seeks to involve those who see themselves as citizens before they do so as partisans of any particular party—or as members of any identity or interest group.

Second: The Third Founding sees itself not as a political initiative but as a search for consensus around a vital public ethics—the broadest and strongest consensus among a diverse American electorate, beginning with the baseline agreement over what is true or false, in the belief that a post-truth democracy is a contradiction in terms.

Third: The Third Founding builds on and supports a broad, if latent, solidarity among the majority of Americans, however obscured and discredited by the far right and the far left, and to do so by restoring a moral language and moral imaginary, humanistic and pragmatic, that counters the warring binaries of today’s culture warriors.

Fourth: The Third Founding rejects the negational political rhetoric of the past half century to advance a positive vision of the future based on local and national civic projects that are unifying and constructive.

Fifth: The Third Founding believes the restoration of a compelling public ethics can be achieved only through the institutions of civil society, precisely because they are the culture-producing institutions, pre-political in nature, in which beliefs, values, and ideas are generated, sustained, and practiced.

Sixth: The Third Founding rejects any forms of political violence, firmly denounces extremists who allow neither deliberation nor compromise, and opposes authoritarians who impose their rule while ignoring the rule of law and the legitimate independence of both government and civic institutions that provide the dynamism of a vital democracy.

We invite readers of this special issue of The Hedgehog Review not only to subscribe to our publication but also to consider joining and supporting the Third Founding initiative—the only effort among many to address our current crisis of democracy at its roots.
